passage: Project log, site 14. Written by Vidya Kulkarni, project head. On Tuesday the contractor wanted the night crew up on the scaffolds during the storm warning. It was within the permit, and the crew leader said his men needed the overtime. Pranav, our junior site engineer, refused to sign the shift sheet. He said, "The permit allows it, but I won't send people up where I wouldn't go myself. Their lives aren't worth less because they are paid by the day." The contractor complained to head office, and Pranav lost his quarterly bonus for delaying the pour. He knew that would happen and did not argue the penalty. I don't think Pranav is some kind of saint; last month he rushed his paperwork like everyone else. But on Tuesday he held a line on principle. I have asked head office to review storm permits.

qa.q: What did the contractor want the night crew to do on Tuesday?
qa.a: To be up on the scaffolds during the storm warning.

qa.q: What did Pranav feel about the day-paid workers, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt protective of them, believing their lives were worth no less than anyone's; he said he wouldn't send people up where he wouldn't go himself.

qa.q: What choice did Vidya make after Tuesday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Vidya asked head office to review storm permits, which could turn one person's stand into a safer rule for every crew.

qa.q: How might the crew leader see Pranav's refusal?
qa.a: The crew leader may be torn: relieved the men stayed safe, yet frustrated that they lost overtime they needed.

grounding: A young engineer acts on a principle of human dignity against a permit and the contractor's wishes and accepts losing his bonus, while the note shows he is not always at that level.

passage: Wednesday night. Today I said no to Deepak for the first time. The flood pictures came in: a mother on a rooftop holding her child's slipper, her face clear, crying. Deepak wanted it for the front page. It is legal; the photographer shot it in a public place, and the whole desk agreed it would sell. I kept thinking: she never agreed to become the face of this. Her grief isn't ours to use. I asked for the picture of the water and the empty street instead. Deepak said I'd lost my nerve and took me off the flood series. That stung more than I expected. I'm no hero; most days I just go along with the desk. But tonight I know exactly why I said no, and I would say it again. - Vikas

qa.q: What did Vikas ask for instead of the mother's picture?
qa.a: The picture of the water and the empty street.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel while looking at the flood picture?
qa.a: Vikas felt uneasy about using it, thinking the mother never agreed to become the face of the story and her grief wasn't theirs to use.

qa.q: What choice did Vikas make, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Vikas refused to run the mother's photo and offered another, and the cost was being taken off the flood series.

qa.q: How might the mother in the photograph have been affected if the picture had run on the front page?
qa.a: Her private grief would have become a public image without her consent, at one of the worst moments of her life.

grounding: A young journalist acts on a self-chosen principle of dignity against the law's permission and the desk's wishes, accepts the cost, and admits it is not how they usually act.

Aparna: heard you got fined by the society??
Rukmini: yes. 500 rupees
Aparna: for what
Rukmini: I came up in the main lift with Lakshmi akka. new rule says helpers use the service lift only
Aparna: ok but the committee voted on it. couldn't you argue at the meeting instead
Rukmini: I did argue at the meeting. lost 40 to 3
Rukmini: she has worked in this building for 20 years. she isn't less of a person because she cooks for us
Aparna: the committee will be furious with you now
Rukmini: probably. I'll pay the fine every time, and I'll raise it at every meeting
Aparna: honestly I don't know if I could do that
Rukmini: I don't always either. I let a lot of things slide. not this one
Aparna: ok. proud of you. a bit scared for you too

qa.q: How did the vote at the meeting go?
qa.a: Lost 40 to 3.

qa.q: What does Aparna's last message suggest Aparna feels?
qa.a: Aparna feels proud of Rukmini and also a bit scared for Rukmini, because of the cost of standing against the building.

qa.q: What choice did Rukmini make after losing the vote, and what does it involve?
qa.a: Rukmini chose to keep riding the main lift with Lakshmi akka, pay the fine every time and raise it at every meeting, accepting the cost openly.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi akka feel riding up in the main lift with Rukmini?
qa.a: She might feel respected after twenty years in the building, though perhaps also uneasy about the trouble it causes Rukmini.

grounding: A young adult acts on a principle of human dignity against a society rule and accepts repeated fines, while admitting they do not always act this way.

passage:
When Dolma's son was arrested in town, the village council in Kaza decided her family would not draw from the common tap until the case was over. "We don't want trouble here," the headman said. No one argued.
Sahil, twenty-five, taught at the village school. Next morning he walked with Dolma to the tap, filled her two cans, and carried one home for her. At the council he said, "Her grandson is in my class. He is not accused of anything. Nor is she. Water is not a reward for good behaviour."
The council fined him, and his landlord asked him to find another room. He paid, packed, and moved into a draughty storeroom behind the school.
He was no saint about it. At night he lay awake wondering whether his mother would be ashamed of the gossip, and whether he had been proud rather than right. In the morning he carried the cans again.

qa.q: What did the village council decide about Dolma's family?
qa.a: It decided her family would not draw from the common tap until the case was over.

qa.q: What was Sahil worried about at night, even while he kept carrying the cans?
qa.a: He worried his mother would be ashamed of the gossip, and whether he had been proud rather than right.

qa.q: What was Sahil's turning-point choice, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He chose to fetch water with Dolma openly and tell the council why, and it cost him a fine and his room.

qa.q: How might Dolma's grandson see Sahil after this?
qa.a: He might see his teacher as someone who treated his family as people when the village turned away, and that could stay with him a long time. 🤍

grounding: A young teacher acts on his own principle of dignity against the village council's ban, accepts the fine and loss of his room, and still doubts himself.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
The council notice on the park railings in Nairobi was new: no food handouts without a permit, and a fine for anyone who ignored it. The permit list had a two-year wait.
Wanjiru, twenty-six, had shared her lunch there with the same three street boys every Friday for a year. Her flatmate Mina read the notice aloud. "You'll get fined. People at your office already think you're mad."
"They're children, Mina. I'm not going to make them watch me eat."
On Friday an officer wrote her the fine. Wanjiru paid it that afternoon and that night wrote to her ward councillor asking for a simple permit for small, one-person sharing.
Mina teased her about being a saint. Wanjiru laughed. "Saints don't check their bank balance twice after a fine. Most days I follow rules just to stay out of trouble, like everyone."

qa.q: How long was the wait on the permit list?
qa.a: The permit list had a two-year wait.

qa.q: Why did Wanjiru keep sharing her lunch after the notice went up?
qa.a: She felt protective of the boys and cared more that children shouldn't have to watch her eat than about the fine or her office's opinion.

qa.q: Besides paying the fine, what step did Wanjiru take, and why is it a sensible choice?
qa.a: She wrote to her ward councillor asking for a simple permit for small sharing, which works to change the rule rather than only defying it.

qa.q: How does Mina's view of Wanjiru's choice differ from Wanjiru's own?
qa.a: Mina sees risk and a reputation for being mad and jokes about sainthood, while Wanjiru sees an ordinary person who mostly follows rules but won't bend on this one.

grounding: A young woman acts on her principle of human dignity against a feeding by-law, accepts the fine, and admits that most days she follows rules like anyone.
